newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Afghan refugees entering Turkmenistan - Red Cross.
newsitem.headline: Afghan refugees entering Turkmenistan - Red Cross.

text.p: About 800 Afghan refugees fleeing fighting in the west of their country have entered Turkmenistan and 18,000 more could follow them over the border, the International Federation of the Red Cross said on Thursday.

"We have information that around 800 refugees have crossed so far," Thorir Gudmundsson, Central Asia spokesman for the relief agency, said. "The potential is for 18,000 more if fighting continues," he told Reuters in Almaty, the Kazakh capital.

On Wednesday, Mullah Yar Muhammad, governor of Herat in western Afghanistan which is held by the radical Islamic Taleban militia, said on Wednesday that thousands of displaced Afghans could die unless international relief was sent.

He told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press that 50,000 people had been displaced by fighting in the neighbouring province of Badghis and many of them lacked food or shelter against the region's harsh winter.
Gudmundsson said the refugees had crossed the Murghab River into the former Soviet republic of Turkmenistan.
Muhammed had said the most vulnerable were located in the remote Bala Murghab area, about 180 km (110 miles) northeast of Herat, where it was difficult to deliver relief supplies.
Gudmundsson said his agency's information was sketchy. "We first need to send people to the area to assess how large the problem is," he said.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees estimates that up to 50,000 Afghans may have fled their homes in Badghis to escape recent fighting between the Taleban and the forces of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Taleban forces are trying to push east through Badghis into Dostum's northern heartland.
A Taleban defeat could make Herat vulerable to a defeat by Dostum and his allies.
U.N. sources say both sides have used planes, tanks and heavy artillery in seesaw battles that have raged along the Murghab river and elsewhere for most of this month.
Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan all share borders with the war-torn country while substantial groups of ethnic Turkmens, Uzbeks and Tajiks live in Afghanistan.

Central Asian leaders, deeply distrustful of radical Islam, held a special summit in the Kazakh capital Almaty last month to discuss the Afghan crisis where they expressed fears of a Taleban advance towards their borders.
Continued fighting in Afghanistan has also placed a big question mark over ambitious plans to construct oil and gas pipelines from energy-rich Turkmenistan to Pakistan through Afghanistan.
